To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the EMU is a monetary union of the eleven Ins and those Outs which have already met the Maastricht criteria.

(i) ERM-II is not the right monetary framework for the European Peripheral countries on the road to EMU; (ii) inflation targeting with an independent central bank is the right monetary framework; (iii) inflation targeting with a differential inflation target is the best monetary framework.

(i) the EMU should be expanded to include all EU countries that meet the Maastricht convergence criteria; (ii) ERM-II participation does not make sense for those EU candidates that have recently applied for membership; (iii) the European Periphery should adopt explicit inflation targets; and (iv) the central bank should be granted full independence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the design of a monetary regime for those countries at European Periphery that are on the road to EMU.
the monetary policy issues that are likely to arise in the process of transition to the euro for countries at the European periphery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the best way of achieving price stability for the European Peripheries is to adopt inflation targeting and grant political and economic independence (possibly with differential inflation targets) to a central bank that has the sole mandate of achieving price stability.

the adoption of explicit, formal, possible differential inflation targets together with a politically and economically independent central bank is the only feasible monetary policy regime that could lead to the successful adoption of the Euro for the European Peripheries.

the adoption of explicit inflation targets is the only way to achieve price stability and a stable nominal anchor in a world of increasing international capital movements and asymmetric shocks, as well as the best way of achieving a credible and sustainable convergence to the EMU.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the European Periphery should not join ERM-II but should rather follow an independent inflation targeting regime.
the European Periphery should adopt a monetary framework that is consistent with the one of the EMU, but it should be tailored to the particular needs of each country.
the European Periphery should not participate in the ERM-II and should not peg to the euro, but should adopt explicit and formal inflation targeting with the aim of achieving price stability.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the European Periphery should be granted a monetary regime that is consistent with the economic and political environment in which they operate and that the adoption of explicit inflation targeting is a necessary step in this direction.

the adoption of inflation targeting is the best option for those countries at Europe’s Periphery that want to adopt a credible and efficient monetary policy framework on the road to full EMU participation.

the European Periphery can achieve price stability in the long run, provided that it adopts a consistent monetary policy framework, which is credible and consistent with the long run goal of joining the EMU.
